title: Taken Up, and Waiting
sum: Luke opens his second book by pointing back to the first: the Gospel told what Jesus "began to do and to teach." For forty days the risen Jesus shows himself alive, eats with the apostles and teaches about the kingdom of God. He tells them to wait in Jerusalem for the Father's promise, the Holy Spirit. When they ask if he will now restore the kingdom to Israel, he answers that the timing is the Father's; their task is to be his witnesses from Jerusalem to the end of the earth. Then he is taken up, a cloud hides him, and two men in white promise he will come back the same way.

The eleven return to Jerusalem and pray in an upstairs room with the women, Mary and Jesus' brothers. Peter explains Judas' betrayal and death from the Psalms, and the group chooses Matthias by lot to restore the Twelve before the Spirit comes.
readings: Luke presents the chapter as the record of eyewitnesses: proofs over forty days, a departure seen in daylight, a known field in Jerusalem. Historians note that his account of the ascension is the only narrative of it, that Luke's Gospel seems to place it on Easter day, and that his story of Judas differs from Matthew's. Those who trust Luke stress his care with places and people; skeptics see a writer shaping tradition for his purpose.
Read as the hinge of a two-volume story

Literary readers see the chapter as a bridge. It repeats the end of Luke (the promise, the waiting, the ascension) and sets out the plan of Acts in 1:8. The restored Twelve stand for a restored Israel, ready to receive the Spirit at the next great feast.

views.H: The Mount of Olives, the Sabbath walk, the upper room and Akeldama place the scene in a Jerusalem Luke's readers could locate. Twelve as a number for Israel's tribes and lots as a way to let God decide were familiar Jewish practice. Annas' family still controlled the high priesthood, and the believers stay in the city that had crucified their master.
views.C: Critical scholars note that Luke 24 and Acts 1 tell the ascension differently (one day or forty), that Luke and Matthew give two incompatible accounts of Judas' death, and that the speeches are Luke's composition. Some (Lohfink, Pervo) read the ascension as shaped by Greco-Roman stories of heroes taken up; others (Keener, Bock) as tradition Luke received from eyewitnesses and presented in biblical terms.
views.L: Luke begins with a summary of volume one, as ancient historians did, and with an outline in Jesus' words (1:8). The departure scene repeats key words, "taken up," "into the sky," "watching," "cloud," to tie the ascension to Elijah, to the transfiguration and to the return. The restoration of the Twelve, by the end of the chapter, prepares the twelve to speak to "the whole house of Israel" in chapter 2.
views.J: The disciples' question about Israel's kingdom (1:6) is a fully Jewish hope, voiced in the Psalms of Solomon and the daily prayers. Jesus does not deny it. The believers pray, keep the Sabbath limit and count by Jewish numbers; Mary and the brothers of Jesus are among them. Jewish readers would also hear in Peter's use of the Psalms the ordinary Jewish practice of reading Scripture as speaking to the present.
views.T: The church keeps Ascension Day forty days after Easter, and the nine days of prayer before Pentecost (the first novena) imitate the believers in the upper room. The creeds confess that Christ "ascended into heaven and is seated at the right hand of the Father." Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican readers have long read Matthias' appointment as the beginning of apostolic succession; Chrysostom praised Peter for acting with the consent of all.

deep.b:
Matthew says Judas returned the thirty silver coins to the chief priests, threw them into the sanctuary, and hanged himself; the priests used the money to buy a potter's field as a burial place for strangers, which is why it is called the Field of Blood (Matthew 27:3–10). Acts says Judas acquired a plot with his pay, fell headlong, burst open, and that the place became known as Akeldama, Field of Blood (1:18–19).

The two agree on the main points: a field bought with the betrayal money, its name, and Judas' sudden, shameful death. They differ on who bought it and how he died. Harmonizers since the early church have proposed that the priests bought the field in Judas' name, and that the body of the hanged man fell and burst. Most critical scholars think the stories developed separately to explain a field in Jerusalem known by that grim name, each tied to a different Scripture: Zechariah 11 and Jeremiah in Matthew, Psalms 69 and 109 here. A third, more lurid version comes from Papias, who said Judas swelled until he could not pass where a wagon could.

Neither account explains why Judas did it. Luke says only that "Satan entered into Judas" (Luke 22:3) and that he went "to his own place."

deep.title: Claude's theory: five looks at the ascension, and Elisha's condition
deep.b: In 2 Kings 2:10 Elijah tells Elisha that he will receive a double share of his spirit only if he sees Elijah being taken. Luke's ascension scene mentions seeing five times in three verses: "while they looked on," "their eyes," "they kept their eyes fixed," "staring up," and "you saw him go" (1:9–11). My suggestion is that this heaping up of sight words is meant to signal Elisha's condition: the apostles have seen their master taken up, so they qualify to receive his Spirit, which comes ten days later (2:4), as Elisha received Elijah's spirit and took up his cloak (2 Kings 2:13–15). The Elijah-Elisha pattern in Luke-Acts is well studied (Thomas Brodie and others), and many commentators link the ascension to 2 Kings 2; the specific reading of the repeated sight words as Elisha's condition is my own proposal.

echoes: Luke 1:1–4; Luke 24:44–53; 2 Kings 2:9–15; Isaiah 49:6; Daniel 7:13; Zechariah 14:4; Psalm 69:25; Psalm 109:8; Matthew 27:3–10; Proverbs 16:33; Luke 6:13–16; Luke 22:28–30

settings.what: Luke's preface to his second book
settings.to: Theophilus, the same patron addressed in Luke 1:3, and through him the churches that would read and copy the book
settings.when: Written after the Gospel of Luke; the dates proposed run from about AD 62 to the early 100s, most often AD 80–90
settings.why: To link the two volumes into one story: what Jesus began, he continues through the Spirit-filled apostles. Summing up the first book and repeating the promise of the Spirit, Luke prepares Theophilus to read Acts as the fulfillment of Jesus' own plan, not as a new movement founded by men.
settings.readers: For believers a generation or more after the events, many of them Gentiles far from Jerusalem, the preface gives assurance (Luke 1:4) that their faith rests on an unbroken chain from Jesus to the apostles to them.

settings.what: Jesus' last words to the apostles
settings.to: The eleven apostles, gathered at a meal and then on the Mount of Olives
settings.when: During the forty days, ending on the day of the ascension
settings.why: To keep them in Jerusalem until the Spirit comes, to redirect their question about the timing of Israel's kingdom, and to give them their life's task: to be his witnesses in ever-widening circles. The command "wait" matters: the mission must begin with God's power, not their own plans.
settings.readers: Luke's readers would see their own churches, far from Judea, as the fruit of 1:8, and read the rest of Acts as the record of the promise coming true.
views: Some read 1:8 as a commission to the apostles alone, fulfilled by their witness, which the church then hands on.
Most missionary movements read it as a charter for every believer and every generation.

settings.what: The messengers' promise of Jesus' return
settings.by: Two men in white, heavenly messengers
settings.when: Immediately after the ascension, as they stand staring upward
settings.why: To turn them from gazing at the sky back to their task, and to assure them that Jesus' departure is not the end: he will come again in the same way.
settings.readers: Luke's readers, waiting for the Lord's return longer than the first believers had expected, are told both that he will come and that the time between is for witness.

settings.to: The believers gathered in Jerusalem, about 120 people, addressed as "brothers"
settings.why: To explain the scandal of Judas' betrayal as something Scripture foretold, and to lead the group to restore the Twelve, the number of Israel's tribes, before the Spirit comes. Peter sets the qualifications: an eyewitness from John's baptism to the ascension.
settings.readers: For Luke's readers the speech answers a question outsiders surely asked: how could one of Jesus' own chosen twelve betray him? It also shows Peter restored to leadership after his denial.

settings.to: The Lord, "you know every heart": probably Jesus, who chose the apostles (1:2), or God
settings.when: After two candidates are put forward
settings.why: To hand the final choice to the Lord. They narrow the field by their own judgment, then ask the one who knows hearts to show his choice through the lot.
settings.readers: Readers learn that the church's leaders are chosen by the Lord, not merely elected, a theme that recurs at the choosing of the Seven (6:3–6) and the sending of Barnabas and Saul (13:2–3).

traditions.q: Matthias was chosen to fill Judas' place, his "charge" (1:20–26). Do the apostles have successors in the church's bishops?
views: Yes. By divine institution the bishops have succeeded to the place of the apostles as shepherds of the church, and the apostles themselves provided for successors (Lumen Gentium 20; Catechism 77, 861–862). The early example is Clement of Rome's letter, which says the apostles appointed overseers and arranged for others to succeed them.

Yes. Bishops stand in an unbroken succession from the apostles, but succession is not only a chain of ordinations: it is joined to the true faith and to the life of the local church gathered around its bishop.

The Church of England kept the historic order of bishops, priests and deacons, holding that "from the Apostles' time there have been these Orders of Ministers" (Preface to the Ordinal in the Book of Common Prayer). Anglicans differ on whether this succession is essential to a true church or a valued sign of continuity.

The apostolic office that continues is the ministry of preaching the gospel and giving the sacraments (Augsburg Confession 5, 28). Succession is first of all a succession of apostolic teaching; some Lutheran churches, such as those of Sweden and Finland, kept bishops in historic succession, others did not.

The apostles' office was extraordinary and ended with them, since they were eyewitnesses (1:21–22); what continues are the ordinary offices of pastors, elders and deacons, and the apostolic doctrine (Calvin, Institutes 4.3.4–5).

There is no succession of office from the apostles. The Twelve were unique witnesses. Each local church calls its own pastors and deacons, and faithfulness to apostolic teaching, not a line of ordinations, makes a church apostolic.

title: The Spirit Poured Out
sum: On the day of Pentecost, the harvest feast fifty days after Passover, the believers are together when a roar like wind fills the house and tongues like fire rest on each of them. Filled with the Holy Spirit, they speak in other languages, and a crowd of Jews from every nation hears the great things of God in its own native tongue. Some are amazed; others say they are drunk.

Peter stands with the Eleven and explains: this is Joel's promise of the Spirit for the last days. Jesus of Nazareth, whom they crucified, God raised from death, as David foretold in Psalm 16, and exalted to his right hand, as Psalm 110 says; from there he has poured out the Spirit. Cut to the heart, the crowd asks what to do. "Repent, and ... be baptized," Peter answers, and about three thousand are added. The chapter ends with a portrait of the new community: teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread, prayer, shared goods and daily worship in the temple.
readings: Many readers, Jewish and Christian, see Sinai behind Pentecost: the feast that later tradition tied to the giving of the Law, fire from heaven, a sound, one people formed. The Law brought death to three thousand after the golden calf; the Spirit brings life to three thousand. Luke never says this outright, so it remains an interpretation.

Others read Pentecost against Genesis 11: there God confused the languages and scattered the nations; here the Spirit gathers people from the nations of Genesis 10 and makes God's praise understood in every language. The languages are not erased but made carriers of the one message.

A third reading stresses that everyone present is Jewish: the Twelve, restored, speak to "the whole house of Israel" gathered from the dispersion. Pentecost is first the restoration of Israel that the prophets promised; the Gentiles come later, in chapter 10.

views.H: Pentecost was one of three pilgrim feasts, and Jews from Parthia to Rome lived in or visited Jerusalem. The list of nations matches what Philo and Josephus say of the Jewish dispersion. Ritual immersion pools found near the temple's southern steps show how large numbers could be baptized. The believers' continued worship in the temple fits what is known of Jewish piety in the 30s.
views.C: The speech is Luke's composition, as all ancient historians wrote speeches suited to the occasion (Thucydides 1.22), though many scholars (C. H. Dodd, Martin Hengel) find in it the early church's preaching pattern. Critical scholars debate whether Luke turned ecstatic glossolalia into a miracle of languages, whether the numbers are round estimates, and whether "made him both Lord and Messiah" (2:36) preserves an early Christology older than Luke's own.
views.L: The chapter is built in three panels: event (2:1–13), explanation (2:14–36), response and result (2:37–47). Peter's sermon is the first and model speech in Acts: Scripture, the story of Jesus, the apostles' witness, a call to repent. The summary of 2:42–47 is the first of several (4:32–35; 5:12–16) that show the church's life between scenes.
views.J: Every person in the scene is a Jew or a convert to Judaism. Peter argues as a Jewish teacher would, from Joel, Psalm 16 and Psalm 110, reading them with the Greek Bible. The new community keeps the temple's hours of prayer and is "well liked by all the people." Jewish readers have noted that the charge "you crucified" was spoken by a Jew to fellow Jews in Jerusalem, and that later Christian use of it against all Jews was a distortion (2:23 note).
views.T: Pentecost became the third great feast of the church, sometimes called the birthday of the church. Its themes shaped the doctrine of the Holy Spirit in the creeds ("the Lord, the giver of life"), the practice of baptism with repentance, and the pattern of worship in 2:42: the apostles' teaching (the reading and preaching of Scripture), fellowship, the breaking of bread (the Eucharist) and the prayers. Chrysostom preached that the Spirit made fishermen into teachers of the world.

deep.b:
Luke describes three sensory signs (a sound like wind, tongues like fire, speech in other languages) and one effect (a crowd of many nations hearing God's praise in their own languages). Readers have understood the speaking in three main ways. Most church fathers and many today: the believers spoke real foreign languages they had not learned (xenolalia). Some fathers, Gregory of Nazianzus among them, asked whether the miracle lay in the hearing; a few modern readers think the believers spoke ecstatically and each hearer understood. Many critical scholars hold that Luke has turned an experience of glossolalia, like that at Corinth (1 Corinthians 14), into a story of languages, to show the universal reach of the gospel.

The gift recurs in Acts at Caesarea (10:46) and Ephesus (19:6), each time at a new stage of the mission. Pentecostals read Acts 2:4 as the first instance of a pattern: Spirit baptism with tongues as its initial evidence. Many other Christians read Pentecost as a once-for-all event, the giving of the Spirit to the church, which individual believers share when they come to faith and are baptized (2:38). See the card below and the topic page on spiritual gifts.

About a third of Acts is speeches. Ancient historians composed speeches for their characters; Thucydides says he kept as close as he could to the general sense of what was said, while making the speakers say what the occasion required (History 1.22). Scholars are divided on Luke's practice. Martin Dibelius and Ernst Haenchen treated the speeches as Luke's own theology in dramatic form. Others, such as F. F. Bruce, Colin Hemer and Craig Keener, argue that Luke worked from tradition and memory and that the speeches fit their speakers and settings: Peter's early sermons have a primitive Christology (Jesus as God's "servant," "made" Lord and Messiah) and Semitic Greek that differ from Paul's speeches later in the book. Both sides agree that the speeches carry Luke's interpretation of events.

echoes: Leviticus 23:15–21; Exodus 19:16–19; Genesis 11:1–9; Genesis 10; Joel 2:28–32; Psalm 16:8–11; Psalm 110:1; Psalm 132:11; 2 Samuel 7:12–16; Deuteronomy 32:5; Isaiah 57:19; Luke 3:16; Luke 24:49; Luke 24:30–35; 1 Corinthians 14; Romans 10:13

settings.to: The crowd in Jerusalem: Jews living in the city and Jews and converts from every nation, there for the Feast of Weeks
settings.when: About nine in the morning on the day of Pentecost, a few weeks after the crucifixion
settings.why: To explain the strange event (not drunkenness but Joel's promise), to proclaim that the crucified Jesus is risen and exalted as Lord and Messiah, and to bring the hearers to see their guilt and turn. The sermon speaks to Israel as Israel: "the whole house of Israel must know." Knowing the audience matters: "you crucified" is spoken to people of Jerusalem weeks after the event, not to Jews of every age.
settings.readers: For Luke's readers the sermon is the model of apostolic preaching and the foundation of the church's message: the Scriptures fulfilled in Jesus' death, resurrection and exaltation, and the gift of the Spirit to all who repent.

settings.what: Joel's prophecy of the Spirit, as Peter quotes it
settings.by: Joel the prophet, quoted by Peter from the Greek Old Testament
settings.to: First, the people of Judah after a devastating locust plague, called to repent; now, the Pentecost crowd
settings.when: Joel's date is debated (many place him after the exile, about 400 BC); quoted at Pentecost
settings.why: In Joel the promise follows God's call to return to him: after the disaster God will restore the land and pour out his Spirit on all his people, young and old, slave and free, before the great day of the LORD. Peter claims that those days have begun, and that the call to "call on the name of the Lord" now means calling on Jesus.
views: Most Christians read Pentecost as the fulfillment, with the cosmic signs either fulfilled at the cross or still to come.
Some dispensationalists hold that Pentecost was a foretaste, and that Joel's prophecy will be completely fulfilled for Israel at the end.

settings.by: David, as the psalm's title says, quoted by Peter
settings.to: First, the worshipers of Israel who sang the psalm as a prayer of trust; now, the crowd
settings.why: In its own setting Psalm 16 is a prayer of confidence that God will not abandon his loyal one to death. Peter argues that since David died and was buried, the words reach beyond him to his descendant, the Messiah, whom God raised.

settings.to: First, a king of David's line at his enthronement; now, the crowd
settings.when: Quoted at the climax of the sermon
settings.why: In Israel the psalm proclaimed God's promise to the king. Peter uses it to show that the one David called "my Lord" is not David, who never ascended, but Jesus, now seated at God's right hand.

settings.what: Peter's answer: repent and be baptized
settings.to: The hearers whose hearts Peter's words had pierced (2:37), and who asked what they should do
settings.when: At the end of the sermon
settings.why: To show the way back to God for people who had just learned that they had helped kill the Messiah: repentance, baptism in Jesus' name, forgiveness and the gift of the Spirit. The promise is offered to them, their children and those far off.
settings.readers: For Luke's readers these verses became the pattern of Christian beginnings, and the churches still differ on what they teach about baptism (see the card).
views: Most traditions read 2:38 as the normal way into the church for all time.
A word to Israel in a unique moment
Some dispensationalist interpreters read it as addressed to the Jews of that generation, who must publicly separate from the nation's rejection of Jesus.

traditions.q: "Repent, and let each one of you be baptized ... for the forgiveness of your sins ... This promise belongs to you, and to your children" (2:38–39). Does baptism itself bring forgiveness, and does the promise include infants?
views: Baptism forgives original sin and all personal sins, gives new birth and the Holy Spirit (Catechism 1213, 1263, 1265). The church has baptized infants from the earliest times, since they too are born with original sin and need the new birth (Catechism 1250–1252); Catholic writers also point to the promise "to you, and to your children" (2:39).
Baptism is a death and resurrection with Christ that washes away sin; infants are baptized by triple immersion and at once chrismated, receiving the gift of the Spirit, and given communion.

Baptism "works forgiveness of sins, delivers from death and the devil, and gives eternal salvation to all who believe" (Small Catechism, on Baptism). Infants are to be baptized, since through baptism the grace of God is offered to them (Augsburg Confession 9).

Baptism is a sign and seal of the covenant of grace, of being joined to Christ and of the forgiveness of sins, though grace is not so tied to it that no one can be saved without it (Westminster Confession 28.1, 28.5). The children of believers are to be baptized, and 2:39 is read as the covenant promise extended to them (28.4).

Baptism is the immersion of a believer, an act of obedience that pictures faith in the crucified, buried and risen Savior; it does not itself bring forgiveness. "For" means baptism is linked to the forgiveness already received through repentance and faith, and "your children" means descendants who also repent (Baptist Faith and Message 7; Second London Confession 29).

Churches of Christ teach that penitent believers are to be immersed "for the forgiveness of sins," and that baptism is the moment God forgives and adds the person to the church; they do not baptize infants.

Acts 2:38 is the plan of salvation: repentance, water baptism by immersion in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins, and the baptism of the Holy Spirit with speaking in tongues. Baptism with the threefold title instead of the name of Jesus is not accepted.

traditions.q: Is being "baptized in the Holy Spirit" (1:5; 2:4) a second experience after conversion, with speaking in tongues as its sign?
views: Yes. The baptism in the Holy Spirit is distinct from and comes after the new birth; it gives power for witness (1:8), and its initial physical evidence is speaking in other tongues as the Spirit gives them utterance (Assemblies of God, Fundamental Truths 7–8).

The Spirit is given in baptism and, in fullness, in confirmation, which the church relates to Pentecost (Catechism 1285–1288). Charisms such as tongues are gifts the church welcomes and tests, but no one charism is required as proof of the Spirit (Catechism 799–801).

The gift of the Spirit is given in chrismation, right after baptism, with the words "the seal of the gift of the Holy Spirit"; the Christian life is then a growing in the Spirit, not a single later experience.

Every believer is baptized in the Spirit once, at conversion, and so joined to Christ (1 Corinthians 12:13); Pentecost was a once-for-all event in the history of salvation. Many in this tradition hold that the sign gifts, including tongues, ceased with the apostles.

At the moment of new birth the Spirit baptizes every believer into the body of Christ (Baptist Faith and Message 2); later "fillings" for service are repeated. Baptists are divided on whether tongues continue today.

John Wesley taught a second work of grace, entire sanctification, after conversion; the Holiness movement that grew from Methodism called it the baptism with the Holy Spirit, a root of Pentecostalism, though Methodists do not require tongues as its sign.

title: Silver and Gold I Do Not Have
sum: At the afternoon hour of prayer, Peter and John meet a man lame from birth begging at the temple gate called Beautiful. Peter has no money, but "in the name of Jesus Christ the Nazarene" he tells him to walk, takes his hand and raises him. The man leaps up and goes into the temple with them, walking, leaping and praising God, and the people, who have known him for years, are astounded.

In Solomon's Porch Peter explains: not their own power but the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob has glorified his servant Jesus, whom the people rejected before Pilate. They acted in ignorance; now they must repent, so that their sins may be wiped out, times of relief may come, and God may send the Messiah who must stay in heaven until the restoring of all things. Moses and all the prophets spoke of these days, and the blessing promised to Abraham is offered to Israel first.
readings: The healing is a picture of what Jesus' name does: a man who could never enter the temple's courts on his own feet now walks in, praising God. Many readers see Isaiah 35 acted out, and the excluded brought into God's house.
Read as an appeal to Israel

The speech is addressed entirely to "Israelites." It offers the people of Jerusalem a second chance: their act was ignorance, their heritage is the covenant with Abraham, and their repentance could open the way to the final restoration. For Luke, the offer to Israel is real.

views.H: The afternoon prayer at the time of the evening sacrifice, the beggars at the gates, the colonnade of Solomon's Porch on the east of the outer court, and the temple police of chapter 4 all match what Josephus and the Mishnah describe of Herod's temple.
views.C: Critics note the parallel healings by Peter (3:1–10) and Paul (14:8–10), with the same phrase "lame from his mother's womb," and see Luke's design in balancing his two heroes. Some (Torrey) found Aramaic behind the rough Greek of 3:16; others see Luke imitating biblical style. The titles of Jesus in the speech, "servant," "Holy and Righteous One," "Founder of life," are often taken as very early, since they fell out of later use.
views.L: The healing and the speech form one unit, which leads straight into the arrest in chapter 4: miracle, crowd, sermon, opposition. "The name" of Jesus links them (3:6, 16; 4:7, 10, 12). Peter's speech echoes the Pentecost sermon but adds new notes: ignorance, the times of relief, the restoration of all things, and the prophet like Moses.
views.J: Peter speaks as an Israelite to Israelites, invoking the God of the patriarchs and the covenant with Abraham. He calls Jesus the prophet Moses promised (Deuteronomy 18) and treats Israel's repentance as the key to God's renewal, a thought close to later rabbinic sayings (Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 97b). The charge of killing Jesus is joined to "you did not understand" and the offer of forgiveness.
views.T: The church has seen in Peter's "what I have I give you" the true wealth of the church, and the story was used to rebuke worldly power in the church. Theologians debated 3:21 in the Reformation: Reformed teachers held that Christ's body must remain in heaven, Lutherans that the right hand of God is everywhere. Origen and Gregory of Nyssa built their hope of universal restoration partly on the word apokatastasis.

deep.b: Readers since the 1800s have noticed that Acts tells Peter's story and Paul's in matching episodes. Both heal a man lame from birth (3:2–8; 14:8–10), both are honored too highly and refuse it (10:25–26; 14:14–15), both confront a sorcerer (8:18–24; 13:6–12), both raise the dead (9:36–41; 20:9–12), both are freed from prison (12:6–11; 16:25–26). The Tübingen school of F. C. Baur saw the parallels as Luke's way of reconciling rival Petrine and Pauline factions. Charles Talbert and most recent scholars see them as a literary pattern, common in ancient writing, that shows the same Spirit at work through both apostles and gives Paul the same authority as Peter.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the lame brought into David's house
deep.b: 2 Samuel 5:8 records a saying from David's capture of Jerusalem: "No one blind or lame may come into the house." The Dead Sea community applied similar exclusions to its assembly. In Acts 3, the name of David's descendant brings a lame man through the gate and into the house of God, walking and praising (3:8). Luke elsewhere stresses the lame invited to the banquet (Luke 14:13, 21). I suggest that Luke tells this healing at the temple gate as a deliberate reversal of 2 Samuel 5:8: the Son of David opens his Father's house to those the old saying shut out. Several scholars have studied disability and exclusion in this story (for example Mikeal Parsons); the specific link to 2 Samuel 5:8 as a reversal is offered here as my own reading.

echoes: Exodus 3:6; Exodus 3:15; Isaiah 35:6; Isaiah 52:13–53:12; Deuteronomy 18:15–19; Leviticus 23:29; Genesis 12:3; Genesis 22:18; 2 Samuel 5:8; Luke 7:22; Luke 23:18–25; Luke 23:34; Luke 24:25–27; John 10:23; Acts 14:8–10

settings.what: Peter's command to the lame man
settings.to: A man lame from birth, begging at the Beautiful Gate
settings.when: At the hour of afternoon prayer
settings.why: To give him what money could not: healing in Jesus' name. The command "walk" invites the man to act on a power not his own.
settings.readers: Luke's readers learn that the apostles carry on Jesus' own works (Luke 5:23–25), and that Jesus' name, not wealth or status, is the church's treasure.

settings.to: The people of Jerusalem gathered in the temple's outer court, addressed as "Israelites" and "brothers"
settings.when: Immediately after the healing, at the afternoon hour of prayer
settings.why: To turn the crowd's amazement from the apostles to Jesus, to show them that their God has glorified the one they disowned, and to call them to repent as heirs of the prophets and of the covenant with Abraham. The speech blames, but in order to forgive: "you did not understand," and "for you first."
settings.readers: For Luke's readers, many of them Gentiles, the speech shows that the gospel came first to Israel as a genuine offer, and that Israel's place in God's plan was not cancelled.
views: A real offer to the nation
Some (Jervell, many dispensationalists) read 3:19–21 as offering Israel the immediate return of the Messiah if the nation repented.
Others read it as a call to each hearer, with the restoration coming at the end whatever Israel as a whole decides.

settings.what: Moses' promise of a prophet, quoted
settings.by: Moses, as Deuteronomy presents him, quoted by Peter
settings.to: First, all Israel on the plains of Moab before entering the land; now, the crowd in the temple
settings.why: In Deuteronomy the promise answers Israel's fear of hearing God directly at Sinai and forbids turning to diviners: God will send a prophet from among them whom they must heed. Peter claims Jesus as that prophet and warns that refusing him means being cut off from God's people.
views: Many Jewish and some Christian readers take Deuteronomy 18 as promising a succession of prophets in Israel.
Others, including the Qumran community and the Samaritans, expected one prophet like Moses at the end of days.

traditions.q: Does "the restoring of all things" (3:21) mean that in the end all will be saved?
views: The church's councils rejected Origen's teaching of the restoration of all (553), and the church teaches the eternal judgment. Yet Saint Gregory of Nyssa hoped for the final restoration of all creatures, and some modern Orthodox theologians say one may hope and pray for the salvation of all without teaching it as certain.

Hell exists and its punishment is eternal (Catechism 1035). The church prays and hopes that all will be saved (Catechism 1058, 1821) but does not teach that all will be; some theologians, such as Hans Urs von Balthasar, argued that such hope is permitted.

No. At the end Christ will raise the dead, give the godly eternal life and condemn the ungodly to endless punishment. The Augsburg Confession condemns the Anabaptists "who think that there will be an end to the punishments of condemned men and devils" (Augsburg Confession 17).
No. "The restoring of all things" is the renewal of creation and the fulfillment of what the prophets foretold; the wicked will be cast into eternal torments (Westminster Confession 33.2).
No. At Christ's return the righteous will receive their reward and the unrighteous will be consigned to hell, the place of everlasting punishment (Baptist Faith and Message 10).

The Universalist tradition, now part of Unitarian Universalism, taught that God "will finally restore the whole family of mankind to holiness and happiness" (Winchester Profession, 1803), and read this verse in that light.

title: No Other Name
sum: While Peter and John are speaking, the priests, the commander of the temple and the Sadducees, angry that they preach the resurrection through Jesus, arrest them; yet the believers now number about five thousand men. Next day before the high priests' council, Peter, filled with the Spirit, answers that the lame man was healed in the name of Jesus Christ the Nazarene, whom they crucified and God raised: the rejected stone has become the head of the corner, and there is no salvation in any other name.

Amazed at the boldness of these unschooled men, and unable to deny the healing, the council orders them to stop speaking in Jesus' name. Peter and John refuse: they must obey God rather than men. Released, they report to the believers, who pray with Psalm 2, asking not for safety but for courage to speak freely and for more signs. The place shakes, they are filled with the Spirit, and they speak boldly. The chapter ends with a picture of one heart and soul: no one needy, property sold and laid at the apostles' feet, and Barnabas of Cyprus as an example.
readings: The chapter begins a pattern that runs through Acts: witnesses arrested, tried, and freed or punished, while the word keeps spreading. The apostles stand before the same council that condemned Jesus, and Jesus' promise that the Spirit would give them words (Luke 12:11–12) comes true.
Read as a church at prayer

Others center the chapter on the prayer of 4:24–30: persecution leads to prayer, prayer to fresh power, and power to unity and generosity. The believers interpret their trouble through Scripture and leave judgment to God.

views.H: The roles in the scene, the commander of the temple, the Sadducees, Annas and Caiaphas, the Sanhedrin's three groups, fit what is known of Jerusalem under Roman prefects. Annas' family held the high priesthood for decades; the ossuary of "Joseph son of Caiaphas" was found in 1990. The council's limited powers explain why it threatens rather than punishes.
views.C: Some critics think the trials of chapters 4 and 5 are two versions of one event, since both involve arrest, a hearing, a warning and release; others see a legal pattern of warning then punishment. The ideal portrait of shared goods (4:32–35) is compared to Greek ideals of friendship and to the Qumran community, and some doubt it was as universal as Luke's summary suggests, since 5:1–11 and 6:1 show problems.
views.L: Boldness (parrēsia) frames the chapter (4:13, 29, 31) and the book (28:31). The prayer applies Psalm 2 phrase by phrase to the passion, a model of how the church reads Scripture. Barnabas is introduced here as a positive example, preparing for the negative one of Ananias and Sapphira (5:1–11) and for his later role with Paul.
views.J: The dispute is an inner-Jewish one: priests and Sadducees, who denied the resurrection, against Galilean followers of a crucified teacher who preach it. The Pharisees, who believed in resurrection, are not named here and later defend the apostles (5:34). The believers pray to the "Master" who made heaven and earth in words taken from Israel's Scriptures, and their sharing fulfills Deuteronomy 15:4.
views.T: "We must obey God rather than men" (4:19; 5:29) became a charter for Christian conscience before rulers. 4:12 is central to Christian teaching on Christ as the one Savior, read differently by exclusivists and inclusivists. The common life of 4:32 inspired monasticism (Basil, Augustine's Rule), the Hutterites and many intentional communities.

deep.h: Sharing goods: Qumran, the Greeks and Acts
deep.b:
Luke describes the Jerusalem believers twice as holding all things in common (2:44–45; 4:32–35). Three backgrounds help. The Greek ideal: philosophers from Pythagoras to Aristotle praised friendship in which "friends' things are common" and friends are "one soul"; Luke's wording would remind educated readers of this. The Law: Deuteronomy 15:4 promised that there would be no one in need among God's people, and Luke quotes its rare word. Qumran: the Community Rule required a new member to hand over his property to the community after a probation period (1QS 6:19–22), and Josephus says the Essenes held goods in common.

Acts differs from Qumran in being voluntary and in leaving people their homes (12:12). Peter tells Ananias that his land was his to keep and its price his to use (5:4). Brian Capper and others think the Jerusalem church may have had a formal common fund modeled on Essene practice; others see a spontaneous generosity that did not last, since Paul later collects money for the poor among the saints in Jerusalem (Romans 15:26).

echoes: Psalm 118:22; Psalm 2:1–2; Exodus 20:11; Deuteronomy 15:4; Luke 12:11–12; Luke 20:17; Luke 21:12–15; Luke 22:66; Luke 23:6–12; John 11:47; 1 Peter 2:4–8; Daniel 3:16–18

settings.by: Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit
settings.to: The rulers, elders and scribes of the Jerusalem council, with Annas, Caiaphas and the high priestly families
settings.when: The morning after the arrest, at a formal hearing
settings.why: To answer the council's question, "by what power or name," and to turn the hearing into testimony: the healing was done by the name of the Jesus they crucified and God raised. Quoting Psalm 118:22 to the "builders" themselves, Peter tells the leaders that they rejected God's chosen stone, and that salvation is found only in his name.
settings.readers: For Luke's readers, who might face courts of their own, Peter shows how a believer answers authorities: respectfully, by the Spirit, and without retreating from Jesus' name.

settings.to: One another, after sending the apostles out
settings.when: During the hearing, in closed session
settings.why: To find a way to stop the movement without denying a public miracle or angering the people. They settle on threats.
settings.readers: Luke lets his readers overhear the closed session to show that the leaders could not deny the facts, only try to silence them.

settings.when: After the council orders them not to speak or teach in Jesus' name
settings.why: To refuse respectfully but plainly: they cannot obey a command that contradicts God's, and they cannot stop telling what they saw and heard. They leave the council to judge.
settings.readers: The words gave later Christians a principle for conscience under rulers, and Luke's readers a model of courage.

settings.what: The believers' prayer for courage to speak
settings.by: The gathered believers, praying together "with one mind"
settings.to: God, addressed as "Master," Creator of heaven, earth and sea
settings.when: After Peter and John report the council's threats
settings.why: To place the threats in God's hands: they read Psalm 2 as foretelling the alliance of Herod, Pilate, Gentiles and Israel against Jesus, and see even that as within God's plan. They ask not for protection or revenge but for freedom and courage to speak and for healing and signs in Jesus' name.
settings.readers: Luke offers the prayer as a pattern for persecuted churches: begin with God's power over creation and history, read the crisis through Scripture, and ask for faithfulness.

settings.by: David, as the believers say, through the Holy Spirit
settings.to: First, Israel at the crowning of a king of David's line, facing rebellious vassal nations; now, the church
settings.why: In its setting the psalm warns rebel kings that God laughs at their plots and has installed his king on Zion. The believers find its "kings," "rulers," "nations" and "peoples" in the passion of Jesus, the Lord's anointed.

traditions.q: "And there is no salvation in anyone else" (4:12). Can people who never hear of Jesus be saved?
views: Salvation comes only through Christ (Dominus Iesus), yet those who, through no fault of their own, do not know the gospel but seek God sincerely and try to do his will by the light of conscience may attain salvation by his grace (Lumen Gentium 16; Catechism 847).
Salvation is in Christ and in his church; the Orthodox decline to say who outside it is lost. As Kallistos Ware put it, we know where the church is, but we cannot be sure where it is not.

Salvation requires faith in Christ, which comes by hearing the word; people who do not profess the Christian faith cannot be saved by living according to the light of nature, however carefully (Westminster Confession 10.4). Elect infants dying in infancy, and others incapable of being outwardly called, are saved by Christ through the Spirit (10.3).

Jesus Christ is the only mediator, and it is wrong to say that Christ speaks equally through all religions; the church must therefore proclaim him to all (Lausanne Covenant 3). Some evangelicals are inclusivists, hoping that God may save some who never heard, through Christ; others hold that conscious faith is necessary.

John Wesley held that a person in any nation who fears God and does what is right is accepted "through Christ, though he knows him not" (Explanatory Notes, on 10:35), while urging that the gospel be preached to all.

traditions.q: Should Christians hold their goods in common, as the first believers did (2:44–45; 4:32–35)?
views: The Jerusalem community is the model of religious life, in which men and women vow poverty and hold all things in common (Augustine's Rule; the Rule of Benedict). For all Christians, private property is legitimate but serves the universal destination of goods, so the needs of others come first (Catechism 2402–2405; Rerum Novarum).
Monasteries live the common life of Acts 4:32, as Basil of Caesarea set out in his Rules; lay Christians are called to generous almsgiving and to treat their goods as entrusted by God.

Hutterites have held all property in common since the 1520s as obedience to Acts 2 and 4 and to Christ's call to surrender everything (Peter Riedemann's Account). Mennonites and Amish practice strong mutual aid without full community of goods.

"The Riches and Goods of Christians are not common, as touching the right, title, and possession of the same, as certain Anabaptists do falsely boast"; yet everyone ought to give alms liberally to the poor (Thirty-Nine Articles 38).
The fellowship of the saints obliges them to relieve one another's needs, but it does not take away each person's title to his own goods (Westminster Confession 26.3).

Christians may lawfully hold property, against the Anabaptists who forbade it (Augsburg Confession 16), and the gospel does not overthrow property or civil order but calls for love within them (Apology of the Augsburg Confession 16). Lutheran teachers read the sharing in Acts as a free work of love, not a rule for all.
